newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - T-bond vols bid, no jolt from Aug expiry.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - T-bond vols bid, no jolt from Aug expiry.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options were slightly bid Friday as August futures options went off with less fanfare than anticipated.
"It (expiration) had some effect, but I don't think it had a tremendous amount of impact," said one T-bond options floor broker at the Chicago Board of Trade.
On Wednesday, one player bought about 22,000 August 115 calls but got out of 5,500 of them Thursday, she said.
"I think that alleviated a lot of fears, to see that guy kind of lighten up his hedge," she said. "I think that helped psychologically the market."
"We saw a big drop in call volatility late in the day yesterday, and that indicated to me that people were not afraid of us going to this 115 strike again," she added.
Another broker called the expiry "fairly quiet," agreeing that jitters subsided when the 115 call buyer offset some of his big position. "Those things went out worthless," he said.
Instead, September futures clung near 114-00 most of Friday after trying unsuccessfully to hold above 114-16/32.
"The 114 strike did have the most open interest, net/net puts and calls, so it's not an unlikely place for the market to sort of gravitate," the first broker added.
September bond options vols were unchanged to slightly firmer, using Monday's dates, and quoted at 8.24/8.30 percent.
"It's better bid, but a lot of that's the weekend," the first broker added. "For today's date, vol is 7.89/7.95. We came in this morning at 7.95."
The second broker quoted Sept bond options 114 calls at 8.0 percent midpoint, based on Monday's date.
"It's a little bit better-bid," he said. "They closed Thursday at 7.84 percent midpoint."
Mortgage hedgers were seen requesting quotes in December 10-year note options, in case yields fall further.
In one sizable 10-year option trade Friday, a dealer sold the December 111/112/113 call Christmas tree at a tick.

In the trade, the dealer sold 7,700 contracts of 111 calls and bought 7,700 each of 112 and 113 strike calls, although it was unclear without Friday's open interest data whether the dealer's customer was just rolling out of the 111 strike and up to 112s and 113s.

"Basically, it is a straight long volatility position. It's flat the market, it's pretty flat gamma and it's long volatility," explained the first options broker. "That's a mortgage servicer, coming in buying some convexity." ((DerivativesDesk(312)408-8750)) E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
